status: Mistrial declared Sept. 4, 2026 after a deadlocked jury. Prosecutors say they intend to retry Lindsay Clancy but have not said on what charges; no retrial date set (judge floated March 2027). Motions to dismiss on double jeopardy, for holdout juror records and for a gag order are under advisement; next hearing Nov. 16, 2026. Clancy remains in custody.

hearings.note: Prosecutors sought recordings of the magazine's interviews with Patrick Clancy. The magazine resisted on First Amendment grounds and the dispute delayed the trial. The filings are not public.

hearings.note: Prosecutors sought Clancy's medical records. Argued together with the reporter's notes question. The filings are not public.

hearings.title: First hearing after the mistrial
hearings.note: Defense renewed its motion for a required finding of not guilty and sought release of impounded juror notes and sidebar records. The judge took matters under advisement and set Nov. 2 for the double jeopardy motion, the holdout juror motion and the Commonwealth's gag order request.

hearings.title: Ruling: motion for required finding of not guilty denied
hearings.note: Judge William Sullivan found the evidence sufficient to send the case to a jury and left the criminal responsibility question to the jury.

hearings.note: All three motions taken under advisement. Prosecutors say they intend a retrial; no date set, March 2027 floated. Sharp exchange between defense counsel and the judge over naming the juror in open court.

hearings.title: Scheduled: status / trial assignment conference, 10 a.m.

updates.t: Motions hearing. Prosecutors say the case is headed for a retrial but do not say on what charges and set no date. Judge Sullivan takes the defense double jeopardy motion to dismiss under advisement, along with the defense request for records on the holdout juror and the prosecution's request for a gag order on attorneys' public statements. The judge says March 2027 is probably realistic for a retrial; the defense wants spring. Next hearing Nov. 16 at 10 a.m. Clancy remains in custody.

Judge Sullivan denies the defense motion for a required finding of not guilty, finding the Commonwealth's evidence sufficient to go to a jury and that the criminal responsibility question belongs to the jury given the conflicting expert testimony.

First hearing since the mistrial. The defense argues for a required finding of not guilty and asks that juror notes and sidebar records be unimpounded for a double jeopardy motion; prosecutors oppose. DA Tim Cruz says no decision yet on retrial or charges. Judge sets Nov. 2 for the motion to dismiss, the holdout juror motion and the gag order request. Clancy remains committed at Tewksbury State Hospital.
The judge impounds the juror list indefinitely after a juror's identity is exposed on social media.
Judge declares a mistrial after the jury reports it cannot reach a unanimous decision. Clancy is expected to remain in a state psychiatric hospital. The DA says a retrial decision is coming.
The judge re-instructs the jury on reasonable doubt and directs it to keep deliberating.
Deliberations continue. The jury tells the judge it cannot agree; a woman is arrested outside the courthouse for aggravated intimidation of a juror.
Closing arguments. The judge instructs the jury and deliberations begin.
The judge denies a defense mistrial motion after a rebuttal witness raised religion, and reprimands the prosecution.
The defense rests and the Commonwealth begins rebuttal.
The defense case begins.
The Commonwealth rests its case.
Opening statements. Patrick Clancy begins testifying. Trial video is in the Trial days tab.

Judge impounds the 911 call and autopsy photographs at the request of the father; media may not record or display them. Both could still be presented to the jury and seen by the public in the courtroom.
Jury selection begins. The father of the children files motions to restrict public display of the 911 call and autopsy photographs.
The judge rejects a defense motion to reconsider that offered a written stipulation of involvement.
The judge denies the defense request to split the trial so the jury would decide the facts before criminal responsibility.
Clancy appears in person in a courtroom for the first time since her arrest, at a Plymouth Superior Court pretrial hearing.
Defense attorney Kevin Reddington gives notice that he will pursue a not guilty by reason of mental illness defense.
The defense seeks a change of venue to Boston. Judge William Sullivan denies it.
The court hears argument on the defendant's psychiatric records and the reporter's notes. No public filing.
The New Yorker contests a court order to turn over recordings of its interviews with Patrick Clancy, citing the First Amendment.
The court orders a psychiatric examination of the defendant and approves DNA testing. No public filing.
Search warrant applications, affidavits and returns are unsealed, detailing evidence from the home and her internet search history.
Clancy is arraigned in Superior Court, held at Tewksbury State Hospital rather than a courtroom, and pleads not guilty.
A Plymouth County grand jury indicts her on three counts of murder and three counts of strangulation.
Clancy is arraigned in Plymouth District Court by video from her hospital bed and pleads not guilty.
Callan is declared brain dead and removed from life support. Prosecutors add a third murder charge.
An arrest warrant is issued charging strangulation, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, and two counts of murder.
Cora, Dawson and Callan Clancy are killed at the family home in Duxbury, Massachusetts. Their mother, Lindsay Clancy, falls from a second-story window and is seriously injured.

civil.title: Lindsay Clancy v. her mental health providers
civil.status: Pending. No hearings scheduled as of Sept. 2026.
civil.note: Claims her providers failed to diagnose bipolar disorder and prescribed medications that allegedly triggered a psychotic break. Eleven defendants, including Dr. Jennifer Tufts, Aster Mental Health, South Shore Health and McLean Hospital. In August 2026 several defendants asked for a medical malpractice tribunal; Aster says she never told Dr. Tufts about hallucinations or thoughts of harming herself or her children. Counsel: Rosemary Scapicchio, Andrew Meyer Jr., Bill Thompson.

civil.title: Patrick Clancy wrongful death suit
civil.status: Pending. A hearing on the motion to dismiss was scheduled for Oct. 28, 2026.
civil.note: Alleges Lindsay's providers prescribed many powerful medications that worsened her condition and led to the children's deaths. Four defendants: Dr. Jennifer Tufts, Rebecca Jollotta, Aster Mental Health and South Shore Health. In April 2026 all four moved to dismiss, arguing they owed the children no duty of care and citing the state law limiting mental health professionals' duty to warn. Patrick's lawyers (Todd & Weld) say it does not apply because the deaths were a foreseeable result of the alleged malpractice.

civil.title: How the two civil cases connect to the criminal case
civil.note: Both suits turn on what Lindsay told her providers and what they prescribed, the same questions the criminal jury heard from the psychiatrists. A guide to the duty-to-warn law that could affect both cases.
